questions.question: In pre-industrial rural England, why were cottagers and poor peasants eager to work for urban merchant clothiers?
options: Open fields were disappearing and commons were being enclosed, so small plots could not generate enough livelihood without supplementary wage work
They were legally forbidden from farming wheat
They wanted to migrate permanently to London to become actors
Peasant households had no children or family members to support
questions.explanation: With the enclosure of common pastures and loss of customary foraging rights, poor peasants could no longer survive on their tiny farm plots alone. Advances from merchants allowed whole families to earn cash wages without leaving their villages.

questions.question: In the proto-industrial textile trade, what was the function of a 'stapler' and a 'fuller'?

A stapler was an accountant, and a fuller was a ship captain
A stapler sorted wool according to its fibre, and a fuller gathered or pleated cloth by pleating/cleansing it
A stapler wove fine silk, and a fuller carded raw cotton
questions.explanation: A stapler was someone who 'staples' or sorts wool according to fibre quality; a fuller was someone who 'fulls'—cleans and gathers cloth by pleating.

questions.subtopic: American Civil War Impact on Indian Weavers
questions.question: How did the American Civil War (1861-1865) directly affect handloom weavers in India?
options: American warships blockaded Bombay and Calcutta ports
American soldiers burned all handlooms in Gujarat
Raw cotton supplies from America to Britain were cut off, so Britain bought all Indian raw cotton, causing domestic cotton prices to soar and starving Indian weavers of affordable raw materials
Indian weavers were drafted into the American army
questions.explanation: When the American Civil War broke out, American cotton exports dried up. Britain turned to India for raw cotton, causing raw cotton prices in India to skyrocket. Weavers could not afford raw cotton and were forced to shut their looms.

questions.subtopic: Yarn to Cloth Transition in Indian Mills
questions.question: Why did early Indian cotton mills focus on spinning yarn rather than weaving cloth, and what forced them to switch to cloth production after 1906?
options: Handlooms were prohibited by law until 1906
Indian mills did not know how to weave cloth until British engineers taught them in 1906
The British government made cloth production illegal
They avoided direct competition with Manchester cloth; after 1906, yarn exports to China collapsed as Chinese and Japanese mills expanded, so Indian mills began weaving cloth
questions.explanation: Early Indian mills spun coarse yarn to avoid competing with British fabric, exporting yarn to China. When Chinese and Japanese mills took over the China market, Indian mills shifted to weaving finished cloth, aided by the Swadeshi boycott.
